:::{#def-differentiable-on}
#### Differentiable on an interval

A function $f$ is **differentiable on** an interval
if it is differentiable (@def-differentiable) at every interior point of the interval;
at a closed endpoint, the appropriate one-sided derivative is used.

[@larsonCalc11e, Section 2.1, p. 100]

:::

{{< slidebreak >}}

:::{#exm-differentiable-on}
#### Differentiable on one interval but not another

- $f(x) = x^2$ is differentiable on $[0, 1]$:
  the computation of @exm-differentiable with $3$ replaced by any $c$
  gives $\tfrac{f(c + h) - f(c)}{h} = 2c + h$, which tends to $2c$,
  including the one-sided limits at the endpoints $0$ and $1$.
- $g(x) = \sqrt[3]{x}$ is differentiable on $[1, 2]$,
  but not on $[-1, 1]$: the point $0$ is interior to $[-1, 1]$,
  and @exm-differentiable shows $g$ is not differentiable there.

:::

{{< slidebreak >}}

:::{#def-continuous}
#### Continuous function

A function $f$ is **continuous at** $x = c$ if all three conditions hold:

1. $f(c)$ is defined,
2. $\lim_{x \to c} f(x)$ exists, and
3. $\lim_{x \to c} f(x) = f(c)$.

[@larsonCalc11e, Section 1.4, p. 73]

:::

{{< slidebreak >}}

:::{#exm-continuous}
#### A continuous function, and one failure of each condition

- $f(x) = x^2$ is continuous at $c = 1$:
  $f(1) = 1$ is defined, and $\lim_{x \to 1} x^2 = 1 = f(1)$.
- $g(x) = \tfrac{x^2 - 1}{x - 1}$ fails condition 1 at $c = 1$:
  $g(1)$ is not defined (it would divide by zero),
  even though $\lim_{x \to 1} g(x) = \lim_{x \to 1} (x + 1) = 2$ exists
  ($x^2 - 1 = (x - 1)(x + 1)$, and the factor $x - 1$ cancels for $x \ne 1$).
- The step function $H(x) = 1$ for $x \ge 0$ and $H(x) = 0$ for $x < 0$
  fails condition 2 at $c = 0$:
  values to the left are all $0$ and values to the right are all $1$,
  so $\lim_{x \to 0} H(x)$ does not exist.
- $k(x) = x^2$ for $x \ne 1$, with $k(1) = 5$,
  fails condition 3 at $c = 1$:
  $\lim_{x \to 1} k(x) = 1$ exists but differs from $k(1) = 5$.

:::

{{< slidebreak >}}

:::{#def-continuous-on}
#### Continuous on a closed interval

A function $f$ is **continuous on** a closed interval $[a, b]$
if all three conditions hold:

1. $f$ is continuous (@def-continuous) at every point of the open interval $(a, b)$,
2. $\lim_{x \to a^+} f(x) = f(a)$, and
3. $\lim_{x \to b^-} f(x) = f(b)$.

[@larsonCalc11e, Section 1.4, p. 73]

:::

{{< slidebreak >}}

:::{#exm-continuous-on-sqrt}
#### Continuity on $\lbrack 0, 1\rbrack$ uses one-sided limits at the endpoints

Let $f(x) = \sqrt{x}$, the [square root](algebra.qmd#def-square-root), defined for $x \ge 0$.
Because $f$ is undefined for $x < 0$,
only the right-hand limit of $f$ at $0$ makes sense,
and @def-continuous-on asks only for that one-sided limit at the endpoint $0$.
Here $f$ is continuous at every point of $(0, 1)$,
$\lim_{x \to 0^+} \sqrt{x} = 0 = f(0)$,
and $\lim_{x \to 1^-} \sqrt{x} = 1 = f(1)$,
so $f$ is continuous on $[0, 1]$ (@def-continuous-on).

:::

{{< slidebreak >}}

:::{#exm-not-continuous-on}
#### A function not continuous on $\lbrack 0, 1\rbrack$

Let $f(x) = 0$ for $0 \le x < 1$ and $f(1) = 2$.
Conditions 1 and 2 of @def-continuous-on hold,
but $\lim_{x \to 1^-} f(x) = 0 \ne 2 = f(1)$,
so condition 3 fails and $f$ is not continuous on $[0, 1]$.

:::

{{< slidebreak >}}

:::{#def-partition}
#### Partition of an interval

A **partition** $\mathcal{P}$ of a closed interval $[a, b]$
is a finite list of points

$$a = x_0 < x_1 < \cdots < x_n = b.$$

It splits $[a, b]$ into the $n$ subintervals $[x_{i-1}, x_i]$,
of widths $\Delta x_i \eqdef x_i - x_{i-1}$.

[@larsonCalc11e, Section 4.3]

:::

{{< slidebreak >}}

:::{#exm-partition}
#### A partition of $\lbrack 0, 1\rbrack$

The points $0 < 0.25 < 0.5 < 1$ form a partition of $[0, 1]$
with $n = 3$ subintervals,
of widths $\Delta x_1 = 0.25$, $\Delta x_2 = 0.25$, and $\Delta x_3 = 0.5$.

:::

{{< slidebreak >}}

:::{#exm-not-partition}
#### Lists that are not partitions of $\lbrack 0, 1\rbrack$

- $0, 0.5, 0.25, 1$ is not a partition: the points are not increasing, since $0.5 > 0.25$.
- $0 < 0.5$ is not a partition of $[0, 1]$: its last point is $0.5$, not $b = 1$.

:::

{{< slidebreak >}}

:::{#def-mesh}
#### Mesh of a partition

The **mesh** of a partition $\mathcal{P}$ (@def-partition) is its largest subinterval width,

$$\|\mathcal{P}\| \eqdef \max_{i \in \cb{1, \ldots, n}} \Delta x_i,$$

where $n$ is the number of subintervals of $\mathcal{P}$.

[@larsonCalc11e, Section 4.3]

:::

{{< slidebreak >}}

:::{#exm-mesh}
#### The mesh of a partition of $\lbrack 0, 1\rbrack$

For the partition of $[0, 1]$ in @exm-partition,
with widths $\Delta x_1 = 0.25$, $\Delta x_2 = 0.25$, and $\Delta x_3 = 0.5$,
the mesh is the largest of these widths, $\|\mathcal{P}\| = 0.5$.

:::

{{< slidebreak >}}

:::{#def-riemann-integral}
#### Riemann integral

Let $f$ be a [bounded](algebra.qmd#def-bounded) function on $[a, b]$.
For each partition $\mathcal{P}$ of $[a, b]$ (@def-partition),
choose a sample point $x_i^*$ in each subinterval $[x_{i-1}, x_i]$.
The **Riemann integral** of $f$ over $[a, b]$ is the limit as the mesh (@def-mesh) shrinks to zero:

$$\int_a^b f(x)\,dx \eqdef \lim_{\|\mathcal{P}\| \to 0} \sum_{i=1}^n f(x_i^*)\,\Delta x_i,$$

when that limit exists and has the same value
for every choice of the partitions and of the sample points $x_i^*$.

[@larsonCalc11e, Section 4.3, p. 272]

:::

{{< slidebreak >}}

:::{#def-integrable}
#### Riemann integrable

A bounded function $f$ is **Riemann integrable on** $[a, b]$
if the sums $\sum_{i=1}^n f(x_i^*)\,\Delta x_i$,
over partitions $\mathcal{P}$ of $[a, b]$ (@def-partition)
with a sample point $x_i^*$ in each subinterval $[x_{i-1}, x_i]$,
approach a real-number limit as the mesh $\|\mathcal{P}\|$ (@def-mesh) shrinks to zero,
and that limit is the same
for every choice of the partitions and of the sample points.

[@larsonCalc11e, Section 4.3, p. 272]

:::

{{< slidebreak >}}

:::{#exm-integrable-constant}
#### A constant function is integrable

Let $f(x) = 2$ on $[0, 3]$.
For every partition and every choice of sample points,

$$
\ba
\sum_{i=1}^n f(x_i^*)\,\Delta x_i
&= \sum_{i=1}^n 2\,\Delta x_i
&& \text{(} f \text{ is } 2 \text{ everywhere)}
\\
&= 2 \sum_{i=1}^n \Delta x_i
&& \text{(factor out the constant)}
\\
&= 2 \cd (3 - 0)
&& \text{(the widths add up to the length of } [0, 3] \text{)}
\\
&= 6,
&& \text{(multiply)}
\ea
$$

so the sums have the same limit, $6$, for every choice:
$f$ is Riemann integrable on $[0, 3]$ (@def-integrable),
and $\int_0^3 2\,dx = 6$ (@def-riemann-integral).

:::

{{< slidebreak >}}

:::{#rem-integrable-integral}
#### Riemann integrable functions and Riemann integrals

A bounded function $f$ is Riemann integrable on $[a, b]$
exactly when its Riemann integral $\int_a^b f(x)\,dx$
(@def-riemann-integral) exists;
the integral is the common limit of the sums.
For example, let $g(x) = 1$ when $x$ is [rational](notation.qmd#def-rational-numbers)
and $g(x) = 0$ when $x$ is [irrational](notation.qmd#def-irrational-numbers),
on $[0, 1]$.
Every subinterval contains both rational and irrational points.
Choosing every sample point rational gives
$\sum_{i=1}^n 1 \cd \Delta x_i = 1$
for every partition,
because the widths $\Delta x_i$ add up to the length $1 - 0 = 1$ of $[0, 1]$,
and choosing every sample point irrational gives
$\sum_{i=1}^n 0 \cd \Delta x_i = 0$.
The two limits differ,
so $g$ is not Riemann integrable on $[0, 1]$,
and $\int_0^1 g(x)\,dx$ does not exist.

:::

{{< slidebreak >}}

:::{#def-riemann-sum-equal-width}
#### Equal-width Riemann sum

For a bounded function $f$ on $[a, b]$ and a positive integer $n$,
split $[a, b]$ into $n$ subintervals of equal width
$\Delta x \eqdef (b - a)/n$,
and let $x_i^*$ be any point in the $i$-th subinterval.
The **equal-width Riemann sum** is

$$S_n \eqdef \sum_{i=1}^n f(x_i^*)\,\Delta x.$$

:::

{{< slidebreak >}}

:::{#exm-equal-width-sum}
#### An equal-width Riemann sum

Let $f(x) = x^2$ on $[0, 1]$, with $n = 2$,
so $\Delta x = 1/2$,
and take each sample point at the right end of its subinterval:
$x_1^* = \frac{1}{2}$ and $x_2^* = 1$.
Then

$$
\ba
S_2
&= f\paren{\tfrac{1}{2}} \cd \tfrac{1}{2} + f(1) \cd \tfrac{1}{2}
&& \text{(equal-width Riemann sum with } n = 2 \text{)}
\\
&= \tfrac{1}{4} \cd \tfrac{1}{2} + 1 \cd \tfrac{1}{2}
&& \text{(evaluate } f(x) = x^2 \text{)}
\\
&= \tfrac{5}{8}
&& \text{(add)}
\ea
$$

:::
